_meta.description: Pre-parsed AUSTRAC/DFAT financial-crime reference content, extracted once into structured form (the nist-ai-rmf-playbook S3 pattern) and ingested deterministically via transport:s3 + mode:map. Typologies and sanctions regimes are durable structural knowledge; enforcement entries are landmark matters of public record (Federal Court civil penalties). No customer/transaction assessments (those are run conclusions).
_meta.authority: AUSTRAC (typologies, enforcement) / DFAT Australian Sanctions Office (sanctions regimes)

aml_obligations.title: Enrol (and register) with AUSTRAC
aml_obligations.description: A reporting entity that provides a designated service must enrol with AUSTRAC; remittance service providers and digital-currency exchange providers must also register.

aml_obligations.title: Adopt and maintain an AML/CTF program
aml_obligations.description: Maintain an AML/CTF program: Part A (risk-based systems and controls to identify, mitigate and manage ML/TF risk, board oversight, employee due diligence, independent review) and Part B (customer identification procedures).

aml_obligations.title: Customer due diligence (KYC)
aml_obligations.description: Carry out applicable customer identification and verification procedures before providing a designated service to a customer (know-your-customer).

aml_obligations.title: Ongoing customer due diligence
aml_obligations.description: Conduct ongoing customer due diligence, including transaction monitoring, and enhanced due diligence for higher-risk customers such as politically exposed persons (PEPs).

aml_obligations.title: Suspicious matter reporting (SMR)
aml_obligations.description: Submit a suspicious matter report to AUSTRAC where there are reasonable grounds to suspect ML/TF or other serious crime — within 3 business days (24 hours for terrorism financing).

aml_obligations.title: Threshold transaction reporting (TTR)
aml_obligations.description: Report threshold transactions involving physical currency or e-currency of AUD 10,000 or more to AUSTRAC within 10 business days.

aml_obligations.title: International funds transfer instruction reporting (IFTI)
aml_obligations.description: Report international funds transfer instructions sent or received on behalf of a customer to AUSTRAC within 10 business days.

aml_obligations.title: Record keeping
aml_obligations.description: Keep records of transactions, customer identification procedures and the AML/CTF program for 7 years.

aml_obligations.title: Tranche-2 designated services (2024 reforms)
aml_obligations.description: The AML/CTF Amendment Act 2024 extends the regime to 'tranche 2' entities — lawyers, accountants, trust and company service providers, real-estate professionals, and dealers in precious metals and stones — with staged commencement (real-estate and professional services obligations from 1 July 2026).

typologies.name: Structuring (smurfing)
typologies.description: Breaking a large cash amount into multiple smaller transactions to avoid the AUD 10,000 threshold-transaction reporting (TTR) trigger.
indicators: multiple cash deposits just under AUD 10,000
deposits split across branches, ATMs or days
many third parties depositing to one account

typologies.name: Cuckoo smurfing
typologies.description: Offshore illicit funds are laundered by depositing equivalent domestic cash into the accounts of unwitting third parties expecting a legitimate remittance.
indicators: unexpected third-party cash deposits matching an inbound remittance
remitter and beneficiary details mismatch
structured cash credits from unrelated parties

typologies.name: Trade-based money laundering
typologies.description: Moving value through the trade system via over- or under-invoicing, phantom shipments, or multiple invoicing to disguise illicit proceeds.
indicators: invoice price materially diverges from market value
over- or under-shipment vs invoice
circuitous routing through high-risk jurisdictions

typologies.name: Third-party money mules
typologies.description: Recruited account holders receive and forward illicit funds, obscuring the trail. Often students or vulnerable persons recruited online.
indicators: newly opened or student accounts with rapid in-out flows
immediate onward transfers to high-risk jurisdictions
account activity inconsistent with the holder's profile

typologies.name: Shell company layering
typologies.description: Complex or opaque corporate structures with no genuine business are used to obscure beneficial ownership and layer illicit funds.
indicators: opaque or nominee beneficial ownership
no real commercial activity or employees
rapid movement of funds between related entities

typologies.name: Digital-currency laundering
typologies.description: Illicit funds moved through digital currency exchanges, mixers/tumblers and chain-hopping to break the audit trail.
indicators: rapid fiat-to-crypto conversion of cash deposits
use of mixers/tumblers or privacy coins
transfers to high-risk or unregistered exchanges

typologies.name: Alternative remittance (hawala) abuse
typologies.description: Informal value-transfer systems are misused to move value outside the regulated banking channel via offsetting arrangements.
indicators: unregistered remittance activity
cash-intensive settlement
offsetting flows with no underlying trade

typologies.name: Casino and junket laundering
typologies.description: Gaming venues and junket tour operators are used to place and layer illicit funds via chip purchases, minimal play and cash-outs.
indicators: large chip purchases with minimal gaming
cash-out as cheque or transfer after little play
funds linked to junket operators or high-risk customers

typologies.name: Real-estate laundering
typologies.description: High-value property is purchased to place and integrate illicit funds, often via companies or trusts.
indicators: purchase via company/trust with opaque ownership
over- or under-valuation vs market
rapid resale (flipping) or cash contributions

sanctions_regimes.name: Australian autonomous sanctions
sanctions_regimes.description: Australia's autonomous country-based and thematic sanctions, imposed by the Foreign Minister, comprising targeted financial sanctions, travel bans and trade restrictions.
sanctions_regimes.legal_basis: Autonomous Sanctions Act 2011 (Cth); Autonomous Sanctions Regulations 2011 (Cth)
obligations: screen against the DFAT Consolidated List
prohibition on directly or indirectly making assets available to designated persons/entities
prohibition on dealing with controlled assets (asset freeze)
obtain a sanctions permit for any authorised exception

sanctions_regimes.name: United Nations Security Council sanctions
sanctions_regimes.description: UNSC-mandated sanctions given effect in Australian law, including asset freezes and arms embargoes on listed persons and entities.
sanctions_regimes.legal_basis: Charter of the United Nations Act 1945 (Cth)
obligations: do not make assets available to listed persons/entities

sanctions_regimes.name: Thematic cyber sanctions
sanctions_regimes.description: Thematic autonomous sanctions targeting persons/entities responsible for significant malicious cyber activity.
obligations: screen and freeze designated persons' assets
no dealing with listed cyber actors

sanctions_regimes.name: Thematic human-rights and serious-corruption sanctions
sanctions_regimes.description: Magnitsky-style thematic sanctions targeting serious human-rights abuses and serious corruption.
obligations: screen and freeze designated persons' assets

sanctions_regimes.name: Russia and Ukraine sanctions
sanctions_regimes.description: Country-based autonomous sanctions in response to the situation in Ukraine, including extensive targeted financial sanctions and sectoral trade restrictions.
obligations: asset freeze and no-dealing with designated persons/entities

enforcement.issue: Failure to comply with AML/CTF obligations — late/non-reporting of ~53,500 threshold transactions through intelligent deposit machines, inadequate transaction monitoring, and delayed suspicious-matter reports.
enforcement.outcome: AUD 700 million civil penalty (Federal Court of Australia) — the largest civil penalty in Australian corporate history at the time.
enforcement.lesson: Systemic reporting failures and weak monitoring on a new channel (IDMs) drive record penalties; onboarding a product/channel without commensurate AML controls is a material risk.

enforcement.issue: ~23 million breaches — failure to report international funds transfer instructions (IFTIs), inadequate correspondent-banking due diligence, and failure to act on child-exploitation risk indicators in low-value cross-border payments.
enforcement.outcome: AUD 1.3 billion civil penalty (Federal Court of Australia) — the largest civil penalty in Australian history.
enforcement.lesson: IFTI/correspondent-banking reporting gaps and failure to monitor for known ML/child-exploitation typologies carry catastrophic penalties and board-level accountability.

enforcement.issue: AML/CTF program failures across casino operations — inadequate management of high ML/TF risks associated with junkets, high-roller customers and large cash movements.
enforcement.outcome: AUD 450 million civil penalty (Federal Court of Australia).
enforcement.lesson: The gambling sector's AML/CTF program must genuinely address high-risk customers, junkets and cash; a program on paper without effective operation is penalised.

guidance.title: AML/CTF programs guidance
guidance.summary: Expectations for a compliant AML/CTF program — a risk-based Part A (systems, controls, board oversight, employee due diligence, independent review) and Part B (customer identification procedures).

guidance.title: Customer identification (KYC) guidance
guidance.summary: How to identify and verify customers (individuals, companies, trusts) using reliable and independent documentation or electronic data before providing a designated service.

guidance.title: Ongoing customer due diligence guidance
guidance.summary: Expectations for transaction monitoring, keeping customer information current, and applying enhanced due diligence to higher-risk customers and politically exposed persons (PEPs).

guidance.title: Reporting obligations guidance
guidance.summary: How and when to lodge suspicious matter reports (SMRs), threshold transaction reports (TTRs) and international funds transfer instructions (IFTIs) with AUSTRAC.

guidance.title: ML/TF risk assessment guidance
guidance.summary: Expectations for assessing money-laundering and terrorism-financing risk across customers, products/services, delivery channels and jurisdictions, and reflecting that assessment in the AML/CTF program.

guidance.title: De-banking and the risk-based approach
guidance.summary: AUSTRAC expects reporting entities to manage the ML/TF risk of higher-risk customers - including remittance (money transfer) providers and digital currency exchanges - on a RISK BASIS through enhanced customer due diligence and ongoing monitoring, rather than through wholesale de-banking. Indiscriminate or sector-wide account closures push value flows into informal, unregistered or offshore channels (for example unregistered remittance / hawala), REDUCING the visibility of financial flows and undermining AML/CTF outcomes. Entities should differentiate risk at the individual-customer level, retain customers whose risk can be reasonably managed, and document the basis for any exit.

guidance.title: Council of Financial Regulators - policy responses to de-banking
guidance.summary: The Council of Financial Regulators (CoFR), with Government, identified digital currency exchanges, remittance/money-transfer providers and fintechs as the sectors most affected by de-banking. Recommended practice for a bank that decides to de-bank a customer: give clear written reasons, provide reasonable prior notice, follow a fair and transparent process, offer a mechanism for the decision to be reviewed, and collect data on de-banking. Wholesale de-banking of entire sectors is discouraged in favour of a proportionate, risk-based approach consistent with maintaining competition and financial inclusion.
